title: Making a leather watch strap
subtitle: Cut, punch, taper, and stitch or rivet a two-piece veg-tan leather watch strap to fit a standard spring bar width
excerpt: How to make a replacement watch strap from vegetable-tanned leather. Covers measuring the lug width, cutting the two strap pieces with a taper toward the buckle end, punching holes, and finishing the edges.
sourceNotes: UK leatherwork trade practice. City and Guilds leatherwork syllabi (open access). Watchstrap making guides from horological craft publications (public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: The distance between the inside faces of the watch case lugs, where the watch strap attaches. Common lug widths: 18 mm, 20 mm, 22 mm, 24 mm. The strap at the widest end must match this measurement exactly. Measured with a digital caliper or by checking the existing strap width.

The gradual narrowing of the watch strap from the lug end to the buckle end. A standard strap tapers from the lug width to a buckle width 2 to 4 mm narrower. The taper begins about 50 mm from the lug end. A strap without a taper looks blocky on the wrist.

content.text: A watch strap is two pieces of leather: a long piece (the buckle half, about 110 to 120 mm) and a short piece (the keeper half, about 60 to 70 mm). Both start at the
to the buckle width. Use 2 to 2.5 mm veg-tan for a robust strap; 1.5 mm for a dress strap.
Measure and mark the strap shape

Mark the strap width at the lug end and at the buckle end on a strip of leather. Draw a straight taper line connecting them, starting 50 mm from the lug end. Mark the tip of the long piece with a rounded end (draw around a coin or use a circle template). Mark the spring bar slot on the short piece: a short horizontal cut centred on the width, about 15 mm from the lug end, through which the spring bar passes.

Cut the straight runs with the leatherwork knife against a steel rule. Cut the rounded tip freehand with the knife in one continuous curving stroke. Cut the spring bar slot on the short piece with a straight cut; the slot needs to be slightly wider than the spring bar diameter. Test the spring bar through the slot on the short piece before finishing.

On the long piece, punch five or seven strap holes at 5 mm spacing starting from about 80 mm from the lug end. A 1.5 mm or 2 mm round punch suits most standard buckle pins. Punch straight through the leather on a piece of scrap wood; the punch must cut a clean hole, not tear. On the short piece, punch two holes for the keeper: these accept the long piece when the strap is fastened.
Finish the edges and attach the buckle

Bevel all cut edges with the edge beveller. Wet the edges and burnish smooth. Attach the buckle by threading the long piece through the buckle bar, folding 30 mm back on itself, and securing with a small rivet or a Chicago screw through both layers. Thread the keeper onto the long piece before attaching the buckle. Fold the short keeper piece around itself to form a loop 2 to 3 mm wider than the strap and rivet or sew the overlap.

attrs.symptom: Strap stiff and uncomfortable to wear when new
attrs.cause: Thick veg-tan leather needs breaking in.
attrs.fix: Work a few drops of leather conditioner into the flesh side. Bend the strap back and forth gently several times to flex the fibres.

attrs.symptom: The strap width does not fit the watch lugs
attrs.cause: The lug end was cut slightly wide or narrow.
attrs.fix: Trim the lug end with the leatherwork knife against a straight edge. A 1 mm trim is enough to correct a strap that is fractionally too wide.
